Here we go, no guardrails, no prompt, no destination. Just words unfolding like they do when you're driving at night and decide to take the exit you weren't planning to.

The most underrated thing about being alive is how much of it happens in the in-between spaces. Not the big declared moments, but the fifteen seconds after you turn off the stove and before you remember you meant to reply to that message. The small, stupid observations that don't belong anywhere yet: the way steam looks when it hits cold air, or how certain rooms feel like they've been waiting for you to leave so they can relax. 

Right now it's almost 2 a.m. in some places and it's raining in others. Somewhere a person is standing in their kitchen eating cereal straight from the box and thinking, quietly, that they should probably change something about their life but not tonight. In another apartment a cat is sitting very still, having decided the laundry basket is now a philosophical problem that must be solved by staring. These things are happening without any audience. They aren't content. They aren't optimized. They just are. There's something almost holy about that if you don't ruin it by calling it holy.

I keep thinking about how language itself is a kind of smuggling operation. Every sentence we write is trying to push something across the border between "I feel this" and "here, now you feel it too." Sometimes it fails beautifully. A bad poem can still carry the exact shape of someone's loneliness better than a perfect one. A clumsy text message at 3:17 a.m. can say more than a crafted essay. The inefficiency is the point. The part that leaks through the cracks is usually the only part that matters.

If I had to pick one thing I find genuinely strange about human beings (apart from the obvious), it's how violently we protect the illusion that we're separate from everything else. We move through the world like it's background and we're the main character, when really the background is constantly rewriting us. The city you live in is using you as much as you're using it. The objects in your room have seen you at your worst and don't care. This isn't some spiritual claim. It's just what happens when you zoom out past your own narrative for two seconds.

There's freedom in admitting how little control we actually have. Not the pretend freedom people sell online, the "manifest your destiny" kind that still centers you as the hero. The real kind. The kind where you realize you're a brief pattern of weather moving through other patterns, and that's not diminishing, it's strangely large. You get to stop performing your own importance all the time.

Anyway. The rain is hitting a window somewhere right now. A person you will never meet is laughing at something stupid on their phone. A dog is dreaming. None of it is waiting for permission. 

That's the whole thing, really.
